name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,183

clue.text: Many colons could be found in a history of this nation

definitions.text: Many colons could be found in a history of this nation

blocks.note: surface reading: lots of the punctuation mark used in a written history

blocks.clueFragment: colons could be found in a history of this nation
blocks.note: setter's reading: colons are French settlers, who ran this North African country until 1962

explanation.walkthrough: The punctuation reading is the trap. 'Colon' is the French word for a colonist, and it was the name for the European settlers of French Algeria.
explanation.definitionFit: French colonial settlers, called colons, lived in large numbers in this North African country before independence.

clue.text: A Spanish force, joined with the French in a Collins novel

blocks.note: the fleet Spain sent against England in 1588

blocks.clueFragment: joined with the French in a Collins novel
blocks.note: add the French article for 'the' and you get the title of a Wilkie Collins novel

explanation.walkthrough: The grid takes only the Spanish fleet, ARMADA. Adding LE (French 'the') gives ARMADALE, a Wilkie Collins novel, so the second half is a pointer rather than wordplay for the grid letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish fleet of 1588 is the best-known naval force sent by Spain, and its name passed into English.

clue.text: Senior lady stirring up the old 1930s MGM establishment

indicators.note: stirring something up mixes it around, so the following words are rearranged

blocks.note: a grandmother, an older woman of the family
these six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An elderly woman shakes up an old-fashioned Hollywood studio.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer: GRAND HOTEL. The definition is a pun: an establishment can be a hotel, and Grand Hotel was a 1932 MGM film.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand Hotel, the 1932 MGM film starring Greta Garbo, is named after a Berlin hotel, a kind of business premises.

clue.text: Antihero seen on the move in early morning passages of Coleridge, Tennyson and Wordsworth?

blocks.clueFragment: on the move in early morning passages of Coleridge, Tennyson and Wordsworth
blocks.note: surface reading: reading Romantic and Victorian poems at dawn
setter's reading: streets named after these poets, walked every morning on the way to the station

explanation.walkthrough: In the 1970s BBC sitcom The Fall and Rise of Reginald Perrin, the hero walks to the station each morning along suburban roads named after Coleridge, Tennyson and Wordsworth.
explanation.definitionFit: The commuting sales executive of the David Nobbs novels and BBC comedy is a classic weary, unheroic central character.

clue.text: Cunning that’s shown by Weir of Hermiston

blocks.note: arch means sly or knowing
i.e. stands for 'that is'

explanation.surface: Craftiness displayed by the title figure of a Stevenson novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Weir of Hermiston is Robert Louis Stevenson's unfinished novel; its title character Archie Weir is the son of the hanging judge Lord Hermiston.
explanation.definitionFit: Archie Weir is the young hero who gives Stevenson's unfinished novel its title, so the title names him.

clue.text: The dearest of the dear’s woeful sin, I fear

indicators.note: something woeful is in a sorry, wretched state, so the following letters are in disorder

blocks.note: these eight letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A lover confesses an unhappy transgression by the most beloved one.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer: FAIR INES, the beloved lady of Thomas Hood's poem 'Fair Ines', who sails away from the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Hood's poem idolises this woman above all others, so she is the most treasured of beloved women.

clue.text: Deception over a university place

blocks.note: a lie is a deceit
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A fraud committed to win a university place.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means on top of, so the deceit sits above the university letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieu, borrowed from French, means stead or position, as in the phrase 'in lieu of'.

clue.text: Mistakenly intervene, mostly to make up again

indicators.note: something done mistakenly comes out wrong, so the letters are put in a wrong order
mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Butting in by error, largely in order to reconcile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make up again' suggests making friends after a quarrel, but here it means devise afresh.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinvent something is to create or devise it anew, which is to make it up a second time.

clue.text: The best access for TLS Online subscribers and contributors?

definitions.text: The best access for TLS Online subscribers and contributors?

blocks.note: surface reading: the ideal way in to the paper's website
setter's reading: subscribers read the paper and contributors write for it, so both kinds of permission

explanation.walkthrough: Answer: READ-WRITE, the computing term for access that lets a user both view and change files.
explanation.definitionFit: Full computer permission lets a user both view and alter data, covering what readers and writers each need.

clue.text: Library in the same place as your heart, according to Yeats

definitions.text: Library in the same place as your heart, according to Yeats

blocks.note: surface reading: a building full of books

blocks.clueFragment: in the same place as your heart, according to Yeats
blocks.note: setter's reading: the title of a Yeats poem whose words fly till they reach the beloved's sad heart

explanation.walkthrough: Yeats's short poem 'Where My Books Go' ends with his words flying 'Till they come where your sad, sad heart is'. A library is literally where books go.
explanation.definitionFit: A library is the destination for books, and the Yeats title names the place his writings travel to.

clue.text: Gosh! 1A’s in charge of pain

blocks.note: 'my!' is an exclamation of surprise
ALG is the standard three-letter code for Algeria, the answer to 1 across
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: An exclamation at the news that an African nation runs the business of suffering.
explanation.definitionFit: Myalgic is the adjective from myalgia, meaning muscular ache, so it describes something relating to bodily suffering.

clue.text: A prop, possibly for a stock comedy character

blocks.note: surface reading: an object used on stage by a comic actor
setter's reading: a rugby forward who might play for a famous London club

explanation.walkthrough: A prop is a front-row rugby forward, and Harlequins is a London rugby club, so a prop might be a Harlequin. The definition is the masked clown of commedia dell'arte.
explanation.definitionFit: The diamond-patterned servant of Italian commedia dell'arte and English pantomime is one of its fixed, recurring roles.

clue.text: Former spy who wrote an article on forced marriage

definitions.text: Former spy who wrote an article on forced marriage

blocks.note: she worked as an agent for Charles II in Antwerp in the 1660s

blocks.clueFragment: wrote an article on forced marriage
blocks.note: her first play, staged in 1670, was The Forced Marriage

explanation.walkthrough: Answer: APHRA BEHN. 'Article' looks like journalism, but her work on the subject was a stage play.
explanation.definitionFit: The Restoration dramatist spied for the English crown before becoming one of the first professional women writers.

clue.text: Wipe out earth, after ages

indicators.note: after places the first-named word behind the second one in the answer

blocks.note: eras are long periods of time
E is the abbreviation for earth in electrical wiring

explanation.surface: Destroy the planet once the epochs are over.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase something is to delete or obliterate it completely, removing every trace.

clue.text: I’m included in very orderly work in the country that was ruled by Napoleon

definitions.text: the country that was ruled by Napoleon

indicators.note: being included in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: anal means obsessively tidy
taken as written
to farm is to work the land

explanation.surface: A tidy-minded worker in France under the emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: The Napoleon here is not the emperor but the pig who takes power in George Orwell's fable.
explanation.definitionFit: In Orwell's allegory the pig Napoleon becomes dictator of the farm, which the animals treat as their own nation.

clue.text: Behaved badly, or performed in the Cambridge Footlights?

blocks.note: first meaning: misbehaved, played up
second meaning, punning: acted at a university that is 'up' from the student's view

explanation.walkthrough: The Footlights is the Cambridge University comedy club. Students are said to be 'up' at Cambridge, so acting there is acting up.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is to misbehave, and a student performing in a Cambridge revue literally acts while up at university.

clue.text: “For this description of thine honesty? — him! For me, he’s more and more a cat” (All’s Well That Ends Well)

definitions.text: “For this description of thine honesty? — him! For me, he’s more and more a cat” (All’s Well That Ends Well)

blocks.clueFragment: “For this description of thine honesty? — him!
blocks.note: the dash marks the missing words of the line
the play where Bertram curses Parolles as the cowardly braggart betrays his comrades

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: in Act 4 Scene 3 Bertram says 'A pox upon him for me, he's more and more a cat.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing words are a period curse, wishing disease on someone, which completes Bertram's line in the play.

clue.text: Crap deal negotiated for a vehicle that should be cheap

definitions.text: a vehicle that should be cheap

indicators.note: a negotiated deal has been worked over and reshaped, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: these eight letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A rotten bargain struck over a budget car.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer: PEDAL CAR. It should be cheap because it needs no petrol, and also because it is a children's toy.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's toy car propelled by pedals costs nothing to run, so it is an inexpensive form of transport.

clue.text: Writer of a particular type that identifies homes for some fourteen characters

blocks.note: a sty is a pigsty, home to the pigs of 14 down
to list is to itemise or name

explanation.surface: An author of a certain kind who names the animals of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fourteen' points to 14 down, Animal Farm, whose characters include the pigs, who live in sties.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylist is an author noted for the quality and manner of their prose, a distinct kind of writer.

clue.text: Hardy’s jolliest content

indicators.note: the content of something is what it holds inside, so the letters lie within the next word

blocks.note: the letters in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: Thomas Hardy's most cheerful material, rarely found.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist Thomas Hardy is the misdirection: the Hardy meant is Oliver Hardy of Laurel and Hardy, known as Ollie. The definition reads 'Hardy's [first name]'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Hardy, the stout half of the Laurel and Hardy comedy double act, was called by this short form of his name.

clue.text: Aurora Scarlett, Ferber’s girl who laughed

blocks.note: Aurora is the Roman goddess of the dawn
Scarlett O'Hara is the heroine of Gone with the Wind

explanation.surface: Two women's names introduce a novelist's cheerful heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer: DAWN O'HARA. Edna Ferber's first novel was Dawn O'Hara, the Girl Who Laughed (1911).
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Edna Ferber's first novel is named, in its subtitle, as the girl who laughed.

clue.text: Broadcast viewer’s greeting

indicators.note: a broadcast is something sent out to be heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a viewer is one who watches

explanation.surface: A television watcher saying hello on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Wotcha is an informal British (originally Cockney) hello, from 'what cheer'.
explanation.definitionFit: This casual British salutation, like 'hiya', is used in place of hello when meeting someone.

clue.text: Former French colony, a rural paradise — that’s not right

indicators.note: 'not right' tells the solver to take away the letter that stands for right

blocks.note: Arcadia is the idealised pastoral land of Greek poetry
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A lost overseas possession of France was idyllic countryside, but something was amiss.
explanation.walkthrough: Acadia was the French colony in what is now Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
explanation.definitionFit: Acadia was a seventeenth-century French settlement in eastern Canada, later lost to Britain.

clue.text: Secret scheme of German and Queen with pressure group

blocks.note: und is the German word for and
ER is Elizabeth Regina
P is the symbol for pressure
a lot is a set or batch

explanation.surface: A clandestine plan hatched by a German, the monarch and a lobby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German and' is the German word for 'and', not a German person; 'pressure group' looks like one unit but splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: An underplot is a subsidiary or hidden plot, a scheme carried on beneath the main one.

clue.text: “Anyone happy in this age and place Is — or corrupt.” (Roy Fuller)

definitions.text: “Anyone happy in this age and place Is — or corrupt.” (Roy Fuller)

blocks.note: the dash marks the one missing word of the line
the English poet whose wartime poem 'Translation' contains the couplet

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Roy Fuller's poem 'Translation': 'Anyone happy in this age and place / Is daft or corrupt.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is an informal term for foolish or silly, which fits beside 'corrupt' as the poet's alternatives.

clue.text: Guy holding leading role in Love’s Labours Lost?

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: to guy someone is to tease them, as is to cod them
the star takes the leading part

explanation.surface: A man taking the lead part in Shakespeare's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer: COSTARD. Cod and guy are both British slang verbs for mock or hoax. The definition is 'one in' the play: Costard is its clown.
explanation.definitionFit: Costard, the rustic clown, is a character who appears in Shakespeare's comedy of the King of Navarre's court.

clue.text: Heard frequently, a German composer who wrote operettas

definitions.text: a German composer who wrote operettas

indicators.note: heard means caught by the ear, so the words are taken for how they sound

blocks.note: frequently is often, and the German composer is Bach

explanation.surface: A composer of light opera whose works are played a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacques Offenbach, born in Cologne, wrote Orpheus in the Underworld; 'a German composer' does double duty as Bach in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Offenbach, German-born and active in Paris, was the leading writer of nineteenth-century comic operettas such as Orpheus in the Underworld.

clue.text: Lacking sense, one with no objectives in revolution

indicators.note: something in revolution turns right round, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a means one
taken as written
aims are goals

explanation.surface: A purposeless revolutionary shows no common sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking sense' looks like foolish, but the sense lost is smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Anosmia is the medical term for loss of the sense of smell, so a noun naming a missing faculty.
